latin: Difficultas intelligendi et ex parte ipsius intellectus et ex parte ipsius intelligibilis prouenire potest.
translation: The difficulty of understanding can arise both from the side of the intellect itself and from the side of the intelligible object itself.
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-swarm-batch7, from Latin at farmer1998:11882

sources.text: Aristotle, Metaphysics 2.1 (993b4-11), in its common medieval Latin version
sources.pico_relation: Farmer's note quotes the passage as the locus classicus behind this thesis

doctrine: Farmer's note traces the question to exegesis of Aristotle's Metaphysics 2.1, quoting the common medieval Latin version in his own English rendering, which likens the intellect confronting nature's most evident things to a bat's eyes confronting the sun (farmer1998:11906). Farmer calls this 'the locus classicus for scholastic discussions of the limits of human understanding,' and notes that 'the insignificance of those limits for Pico is illustrated in [3>40], which provides his commentary on thesis 7.25 from Averroes' (farmer1998:11906). Edelheit reports that 'Pico in thesis 40 according to Thomas Aquinas simply presents these two options' — that difficulty in understanding may come from the intellect or from the thing understood — without deciding between them (edelheit2022:4119).
context: Edelheit contrasts Pico's even-handed formulation with the Parisian commentary tradition on Aristotle's Metaphysics (via Hennon), which 'concludes that it comes from our intellect' rather than leaving the question open (edelheit2022:4119), and cites a related, anonymous 'Conclusio responsalis' recorded by Bakker's edition of the Paris commentaries, on the difficulty of understanding both material and immaterial substances (edelheit2022:4141).
reception: Edelheit records that 'thesis 40, just like thesis 20, is included among the theses which were criticized by Bernardo Torni', to be discussed 'again and with further detail in Chapter 12' (edelheit2022:12649); the content of Torni's criticism itself is not given in the material consulted.
historiography: Edelheit (2022) reads thesis 40 as juxtaposing, without adjudicating, the two standard scholastic answers to where cognitive difficulty originates (edelheit2022:4119, 12649), against the background of the Parisian commentary tradition that resolves the question in favor of the intellect (edelheit2022:4119).

quotations.text: But perhaps, since a difficulty exists in two modes, its cause is not in things but in us. For just as the eyes of a bat [“owl” in Pico, see 7.25 note] stand to the sun, so too the intellect of our soul stands to those things that in all of nature are most evident.
Thesis 40, just like thesis 20, is included among the theses which were criticized by Bernardo Torni

not_established: The substance of Bernardo Torni's criticism of thesis 40 is not established from the material consulted; Edelheit defers it to a chapter not excerpted in the packet.
Farmer's cross-reference note on 3>40 as Pico's 'commentary on thesis 7.25 from Averroes' has not been independently verified against 3>40's own text in this entry.
